Why does the limit ignore what happens at x = 2?

By definition, $\lim_{x\to 2} f(x) = L$ means $f(x)$ can be made arbitrarily close to $L$ by taking $x$ sufficiently close to 2, **with $x \neq 2$** (Stewart §2.2). The value $f(2)$ never appears in the definition, so it can't affect the limit.

notes.Math/Calculus/Limits.md:
# Limits

A limit is the value of the function at a point.

Example: lim x→2 of (x^2-4)/(x-2) is undefined because you can't divide by zero.

One-sided limits: the left limit and the right limit. If they are different, the limit is undefined.
